title: LazyMem: Retrieve Broadly, Construct Selectively for Efficient Long-Term Agent Memory

images.desc:
3.1 The LazyMem Pipeline


Figure 1: 
Overview of LazyMem.
At query time (top), hybrid retrieval, context windowing, and selective
construction turn a long conversation history into compact memory for the
answer model. The memory-processing model is initialized with teacher-supervised
fine-tuning and refined through reinforcement learning with action and quality
rewards (bottom).



We consider the problem of answering a query qq over a long interaction history,
where the agent must draw on relevant information scattered across past user and
assistant messages.
LazyMem addresses this as a lazy, retrieve-then-construct memory
system (see Figure 1): messages are stored verbatim with no
processing at write time, and all work is deferred to query time, where the
system operates in three stages.


Retrieve broadly.


LazyMem first builds a high-recall pool of at most nn candidate messages,
ℛq\mathcal{R}_{q}, using standard hybrid retrieval.
Dense (bi-encoder) and sparse (BM25) retrievers run in parallel on qq, and their
ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank
Fusion (Cormack et al., 2009); a cross-encoder reranker then scores the
fused candidates and retains the top nn.
All retrieval components are off-the-shelf. The contribution of LazyMem lies in
how the resulting pool is subsequently processed.



Construct selectively.


A construction module then compresses ℛq\mathcal{R}_{q} into a compact,
query-conditioned memory context mqm_{q}.
It partitions the pool into overlapping evidence windows and applies a
lightweight, RL-trained memory-processing model πθ\pi_{\theta} to all windows in
parallel (see Section 3.2).
Windowing caps the number of messages processed per model call while preserving
cross-boundary evidence, and parallelism bounds latency as the pool grows.
Section 3.3 describes how πθ\pi_{\theta} attains high construction
quality despite its small size.



Answer.


Finally, an answer model takes the query qq together with the compact context
mqm_{q} to produce the prediction.

4.3 Efficiency Analysis (RQ2)


Figure 2: 
Accuracy–efficiency trade-offs on LongMemEval.
Left: LJ versus average answer-context memory tokens (log scale); MemT is
omitted because it lacks a comparable token count.
Right: LJ versus mean end-to-end latency under the same serving setup; bars
span P50–P95, and LazyMem uses the 4B memory-processing model.
Dashed lines mark Pareto frontiers (upper left is better). Labels report token
counts (left) and mean latencies (right).



Figure 2 shows that LazyMem offers a strong accuracy–context trade-off, with both configurations lying on the answer-context-memory-token–accuracy Pareto frontier. LazyMem-4B achieves an LJ of 0.850.85 with an average of only 213 answer-context memory tokens, reducing this count by factors of 68.768.7 relative to RAG Top50 and 21.021.0 relative to StructMem, while improving LJ by 0.100.10 and 0.030.03, respectively. Using Qwen3-32B as the memory-processing model further increases LJ to 0.930.93 with 1,041 answer-context memory tokens. These results indicate that query-conditioned construction can substantially reduce the context passed to the answer model while maintaining strong downstream accuracy.


The latency results show that LazyMem-4B also provides a favorable accuracy–latency trade-off. Although it has higher online latency than the write-time methods LightMem and StructMem, it achieves higher accuracy. Compared with NanoMemory, the other query-time construction method, LazyMem-4B improves LJ from 0.800.80 to 0.850.85 while reducing mean end-to-end latency from 55.35 s to 40.86 s, placing it on the latency–accuracy Pareto frontier. Its lightweight trained memory-processing model and parallel window processing keep the additional query-time overhead manageable.

Figure 3: 
Human-attributed errors for LazyMem-4B and the prompt-only 32B
variant, overall and by question type. Triplets denote retrieval miss /
editing loss / QA reasoning (R/E/Q). SSA and SSU have zero errors.



Table 3 shows that cumulative training consistently improves over prompting alone. The final RL model raises LJ from 0.41 to 0.85 on LongMemEval and from 0.56 to 0.68 on LoCoMo. SFT accounts for most of the initial gain (LJ +0.32 / +0.07), largely by eliminating malformed gate outputs (Gate Fmt. jumps from 0.397 to 0.963 and 0.622 to 0.985). RL adds a further +0.12 / +0.05 with negligible format change, indicating that its gains come from improved memory-construction decisions rather than format compliance. This validates the staged design: SFT establishes reliable gate execution, RL refines what to retain.


Complementing the cross-method comparison in
Section 4.2, SSP shows a distinct stage-wise pattern:
accuracy remains at 0.17 after SFT but rises to 0.67 after RL. Because these
questions require converting user history into recommendation-relevant
evidence, success may depend not only on retaining relevant evidence but also on how
it is compressed. The utility reward may therefore improve query-time memory construction by making the compressed preferences more useful for the
current recommendation. Given the relatively small SSP subset, this explanation
remains tentative.
